title: Research: how other cities guide riders underground

questions.question: Has anyone solved underground guidance before?
questions.answer: Yes, in pieces. Tokyo deployed camera arrows, Washington and Singapore deployed phone-sensor guidance, London trialled beacons, and Seoul offers app guidance. Research covers pressure-based floors and iPhone path retracing. Each addresses part of the rider's problem.

sources.title: The guided walk, ideas proven elsewhere

questions.question: How does Washington Metro guide riders underground?
questions.answer: Waymap is deployed across 98 Metro stations. It pairs phone motion sensors with mapped walking routes, the closest published comparison to our phone-sensors-plus-mapped-routes approach.

sources.title: Waymap case study: WMATA Washington Metro

questions.question: What did Singapore deploy?
questions.answer: SBS Transit deployed Waymap at three stations, using the same phone-motion and mapped-route approach as Washington.

sources.title: Waymap case study: SBS Transit Singapore

questions.question: What did London try?
questions.answer: Wayfindr trialled Bluetooth-beacon guidance at Euston, in a major London Underground trial announced by Transport for London in December 2015. Beacons are station hardware; our approach instead uses the phone's own sensors.

sources.title: Transport for London: Wayfindr Euston trial

questions.question: What does Seoul offer?
questions.answer: Seoul's official subway app offers platform and exit guidance, announced for foreign residents and tourists. The city's announcement leaves the positioning method unspecified, so we cannot say which technique it uses.

questions.question: What did Tokyo deploy?
questions.answer: Tokyo's Toei Subway deployed camera arrows at Tochomae: the rider points the camera and arrows show the way. Announced in January 2024, it is the clearest precedent for camera-based guidance underground.

questions.question: Can pressure really tell which floor?
questions.answer: FloorPair tested pressure-based floor identification at two subway stations. It shows calibrated phone pressure can distinguish levels, which supports our barometer step. Our own Queensboro trace shows a climb of about nine metres but still cannot name the landing alone.

questions.question: Can an iPhone retrace an indoor walk?
questions.answer: Clew is an open-source iPhone app that retraces an indoor path using ARKit. It shows consumer phone tracking can work indoors without GPS, which is the tracking step our live guide would need.
